Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year’s wages, which explains the indignation of the onlookers."},{"verse":9,"phrase":"good news","lemma":"εὐαγγέλιον","kind":"departure","traditional":"gospel","note":"The Greek word meant good news or its announcement, such as news of a victory or a ruler’s accession, and the Greek Old Testament uses the related verb for announcing God’s reign. “Gospel” originally meant the same in English but now suggests a book or a religious category. Many modern translations use “good news” in at least some places."},{"verse":10,"phrase":"hand him over","lemma":"παραδίδωμι","kind":"departure","traditional":"betray him","note":"The verb is the ordinary word for handing someone or something over. Mark uses it for John’s arrest, for the Son of Man being handed over to human hands, and for the priests handing Jesus to Pilate. Most translations use “betray” when Judas is the subject, which fits the act but hides that the same word runs through the whole passion story. Greek has a separate word for treachery, which Mark does not use."},{"verse":36,"phrase":"Abba, Father","lemma":"ἀββά","kind":"background","traditional":"Abba, Father","note":"Abba is the Aramaic word for “father”, and Mark gives the Greek translation beside it. It was used by adult children as well as small ones, so the popular claim that it means “Daddy” goes beyond the evidence. It is nonetheless a direct and familiar form of address to God."},{"verse":38,"phrase":"testing","lemma":"πειρασμός","kind":"departure","traditional":"temptation","note":"The Greek word covers both a trial that tests a person and an enticement to do wrong. English “temptation” now suggests only the second. With the arrest moments away, the sense here is the ordeal that will test the disciples’ loyalty. Most translations keep “temptation”; some have “the time of trial”."},{"verse":41,"phrase":"Enough!","lemma":"ἀπέχω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"It is enough","note":"This single Greek word is one of the most obscure in Mark. “It is enough” is the traditional guess; other proposals include “it is settled” and “the account is paid”, the latter from the verb’s use on commercial receipts. The words before it can also be read as a command (“Sleep on now and rest”) and not as a question. No solution has general agreement."},{"verse":47,"phrase":"slave","lemma":"δοῦλος","kind":"departure","traditional":"servant","note":"The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Many English versions soften it to “servant”; several recent ones use “slave”, as here."},{"verse":48,"phrase":"bandit","lemma":"λῃστής","kind":"departure","traditional":"robber; thief","note":"The word denotes someone who plunders with violence, a brigand or outlaw, not a burglar or pickpocket. Writers of the period also applied it to armed insurgents, and some translations render it “rebel” or “revolutionary” here. Mark uses the same word for the two men crucified with Jesus."},{"verse":58,"phrase":"sanctuary","lemma":"ναός","kind":"departure","traditional":"temple","note":"Mark uses two Greek words that English versions usually both translate “temple”. One refers to the whole temple complex with its courts (as in verse 49), and the one used here refers to the sanctuary building itself. The translation keeps them distinct, though scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers observe the difference."},{"verse":61,"phrase":"Messiah","lemma":"Χριστός","kind":"departure","traditional":"Christ","note":"The Greek word translates the Hebrew title Messiah, the anointed king Israel expected. Here the high priest is asking about that title, not using a name, so “Messiah” is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction, keeping “Christ” where it works as a name."},{"verse":62,"phrase":"the Power","lemma":"δύναμις","kind":"background","traditional":"Power; the Mighty One","note":"“The Power”, like “the Blessed One” in the high priest’s question, is a reverent way of referring to God without naming him. Jesus’ answer combines the language of Psalm 110:1 (seated at God’s right hand) and Daniel 7:13 (one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven)."},{"verse":68,"phrase":"and a rooster crowed","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"","note":"These words are absent from several of the earliest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and some critical editions bracket them. SBLGNT prints them. They prepare for the “second time” in verse 72, which may be why a copyist added them or the reason they are original."},{"verse":70,"phrase":"and your speech is like theirs","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"","note":"These words are printed in SBLGNT but are missing from the earliest manuscripts and from most other modern critical editions, and so from many English translations. Many scholars think they were added by copyists under the influence of Matthew 26:73."},{"verse":71,"phrase":"call down curses","lemma":"ἀναθεματίζω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"to curse and swear","note":"The verb means to invoke a solemn curse, not to use foul language. The Greek gives no object. Most translations understand Peter to be calling a curse on himself if he is lying; some scholars argue that he is cursing Jesus. The translation leaves the object unstated, as Mark does."},{"verse":72,"phrase":"he broke down and wept","lemma":"ἐπιβάλλω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"when he thought on it, he wept; he broke down and wept","note":"The Greek participle here literally means “having thrown upon”, and its sense in this sentence is uncertain. Proposals include “he broke down”, “when he thought about it”, “he began to” and “covering his head”. The rendering follows the most common modern choice."}],"candidates":[{"lemma":"παραδίδωμι","rendering":"hand over","verse":10,"reason":"Used across the Gospels, Acts and Paul for Judas, the priests, Pilate and God; whether Judas’s act is “betray” or “hand over” must be settled once to keep the passion narrative’s verbal thread consistent."},{"lemma":"εὐαγγέλιον","rendering":"good news","verse":9,"reason":"Recurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between “gospel” and “good news”; variation between chapters would confuse readers."},{"lemma":"δοῦλος","rendering":"slave","verse":47,"reason":"Very frequent in narrative, parables and Paul’s self-descriptions; “slave” versus “servant” changes the social picture and needs one policy."},{"lemma":"πειρασμός","rendering":"testing","verse":38,"reason":"Occurs in the Lord’s Prayer, Gethsemane, James and elsewhere; “temptation”, “testing” and “trial” give different meanings and should not vary arbitrarily."},{"lemma":"σκανδαλίζω","rendering":"fall away","verse":27,"reason":"A recurring Gospel verb rendered variously as “fall away”, “stumble”, “take offence” or “cause to sin”; it needs a governed set of renderings by sense."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was now two days before the Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to seize him by stealth and kill him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Not during the festival, or there may be a riot among the people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was in Bethany, reclining at table in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came with an alabaster flask of very costly perfume, pure nard. She broke the flask and poured it over his head.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some were saying indignantly to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why this waste of the perfume?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This perfume could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they scolded her harshly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Leave her alone. Why are you making trouble for her? She has done a good deed for me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want you can do good to them; but you do not always have me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: She did what she could: she has anointed my body beforehand for its burial.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, wherever the good news is proclaimed throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went off to the chief priests to hand him over to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this they were glad, and they promised to give him money. So he began looking for a good opportunity to hand him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, his disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He sent two of his disciples and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and wherever he goes in, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says: Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He will show you a large upstairs room, furnished and ready. Prepare for us there.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples set out and went into the city and found everything just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over, one who is eating with me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Surely not I?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “One of the Twelve, the one dipping into the bowl with me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Son of Man goes just as it is written about him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were eating, he took bread, said a blessing, broke it and gave it to them, and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take it; this is my body.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he took a cup, gave thanks and gave it to them, and they all drank from it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, I will never again drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Even if they all fall away, I will not.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, today, this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he kept insisting all the more,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they all said the same.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to a place named Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Sit here while I pray.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He took Peter, James and John with him, and he began to be overcome with dread and anguish,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My soul is deeply sorrowful, to the point of death. Remain here and stay awake.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Going a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass him by.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Take this cup away from me. Yet not what I want, but what you want.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Simon, are you asleep? Did you not have the strength to stay awake one hour?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Stay awake and pray, so that you do not come into testing. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came the third time and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Get up, let us go. Look, the one handing me over has come near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, the scribes and the elders.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the one handing him over had given them a signal, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The one I kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away securely.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he arrived, he went up to him at once and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he kissed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They laid hands on him and seized him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But one of those standing by drew his sword and struck the high priest’s slave, cutting off his ear.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus responded to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if against a bandit?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But this is so that the scriptures may be fulfilled.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they all left him and fled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A certain young man was following along with him, wearing nothing but a linen cloth over his bare body. They seized him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders and the scribes assembled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter followed him from a distance, right inside the courtyard of the high priest, and he was sitting with the attendants and warming himself at the fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus so as to put him to death, but they could find none.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For many were giving false testimony against him, but their testimonies did not agree.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some stood up and gave false testimony against him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We heard him say, ‘I will tear down this sanctuary made by hands, and in three days I will build another not made by hands.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet not even on this did their testimony agree.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the high priest stood up in the middle and questioned Jesus, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you make no answer at all? What is it these men are testifying against you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he kept silent and answered nothing. Again the high priest questioned him and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The high priest tore his clothes and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do we still need witnesses?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they all condemned him as deserving death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some began to spit on him, to cover his face, to strike him with their fists and to say to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Prophesy!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the attendants took him and slapped him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s slave girls came by,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked straight at him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You too were with the Nazarene, Jesus.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he denied it, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I neither know nor understand what you are talking about.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went outside into the forecourt, and a rooster crowed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The slave girl saw him and began again to say to those standing by,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is one of them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he denied it again. A little later those standing by again said to Peter,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You really are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech is like theirs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he began to call down curses and to swear,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I do not know this man you are talking about.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately a rooster crowed a second time. Then Peter remembered what Jesus had said to him:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he broke down and wept.

notes.note: The adjective describing the nard is rare and its meaning is uncertain. Most scholars connect it with the word for “trustworthy” and take it to mean genuine or unadulterated, which is the reading followed here. Others have proposed “liquid” or a trade name for a particular variety of nard.

notes.traditional: three hundred denarii; three hundred pence
notes.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a labourer. Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year’s wages, which explains the indignation of the onlookers.

The Greek word meant good news or its announcement, such as news of a victory or a ruler’s accession, and the Greek Old Testament uses the related verb for announcing God’s reign. “Gospel” originally meant the same in English but now suggests a book or a religious category. Many modern translations use “good news” in at least some places.

The verb is the ordinary word for handing someone or something over. Mark uses it for John’s arrest, for the Son of Man being handed over to human hands, and for the priests handing Jesus to Pilate. Most translations use “betray” when Judas is the subject, which fits the act but hides that the same word runs through the whole passion story. Greek has a separate word for treachery, which Mark does not use.

Abba is the Aramaic word for “father”, and Mark gives the Greek translation beside it. It was used by adult children as well as small ones, so the popular claim that it means “Daddy” goes beyond the evidence. It is nonetheless a direct and familiar form of address to God.

The Greek word covers both a trial that tests a person and an enticement to do wrong. English “temptation” now suggests only the second. With the arrest moments away, the sense here is the ordeal that will test the disciples’ loyalty. Most translations keep “temptation”; some have “the time of trial”.

This single Greek word is one of the most obscure in Mark. “It is enough” is the traditional guess; other proposals include “it is settled” and “the account is paid”, the latter from the verb’s use on commercial receipts. The words before it can also be read as a command (“Sleep on now and rest”) and not as a question. No solution has general agreement.
The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Many English versions soften it to “servant”; several recent ones use “slave”, as here.

The word denotes someone who plunders with violence, a brigand or outlaw, not a burglar or pickpocket. Writers of the period also applied it to armed insurgents, and some translations render it “rebel” or “revolutionary” here. Mark uses the same word for the two men crucified with Jesus.

Mark uses two Greek words that English versions usually both translate “temple”. One refers to the whole temple complex with its courts (as in verse 49), and the one used here refers to the sanctuary building itself. The translation keeps them distinct, though scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers observe the difference.

The Greek word translates the Hebrew title Messiah, the anointed king Israel expected. Here the high priest is asking about that title, not using a name, so “Messiah” is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction, keeping “Christ” where it works as a name.

“The Power”, like “the Blessed One” in the high priest’s question, is a reverent way of referring to God without naming him. Jesus’ answer combines the language of Psalm 110:1 (seated at God’s right hand) and Daniel 7:13 (one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven).

These words are absent from several of the earliest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and some critical editions bracket them. SBLGNT prints them. They prepare for the “second time” in verse 72, which may be why a copyist added them or the reason they are original.

notes.phrase: and your speech is like theirs
notes.note: These words are printed in SBLGNT but are missing from the earliest manuscripts and from most other modern critical editions, and so from many English translations. Many scholars think they were added by copyists under the influence of Matthew 26:73.

The verb means to invoke a solemn curse, not to use foul language. The Greek gives no object. Most translations understand Peter to be calling a curse on himself if he is lying; some scholars argue that he is cursing Jesus. The translation leaves the object unstated, as Mark does.

notes.traditional: when he thought on it, he wept; he broke down and wept
notes.note: The Greek participle here literally means “having thrown upon”, and its sense in this sentence is uncertain. Proposals include “he broke down”, “when he thought about it”, “he began to” and “covering his head”. The rendering follows the most common modern choice.

candidates.reason: Used across the Gospels, Acts and Paul for Judas, the priests, Pilate and God; whether Judas’s act is “betray” or “hand over” must be settled once to keep the passion narrative’s verbal thread consistent.
Recurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between “gospel” and “good news”; variation between chapters would confuse readers.
Very frequent in narrative, parables and Paul’s self-descriptions; “slave” versus “servant” changes the social picture and needs one policy.
Occurs in the Lord’s Prayer, Gethsemane, James and elsewhere; “temptation”, “testing” and “trial” give different meanings and should not vary arbitrarily.
A recurring Gospel verb rendered variously as “fall away”, “stumble”, “take offence” or “cause to sin”; it needs a governed set of renderings by sense.
